entry.title: Orion Belt v1.5.1 — installs on Fedora Atomic
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.5.1 fixes server package installs on Fedora Silverblue, Kinoite and CoreOS, where rpm-ostree rejected the package, keeps the gateway SSH host key stable across OS updates there, and takes in dependency updates.
entry.content:
Orion Belt 1.5.1 is a packaging fix for Fedora's image-based systems: Silverblue, Kinoite and the other Atomic desktops, and Fedora CoreOS.

What went wrong​

rpm-ostree install orion-belt stopped with mkdir: cannot create directory '/var/lib/orion-belt': Read-only file system. rpm-ostree runs package scripts in a sandbox where /var is empty and read-only, and the server package created its data and log directories there.

The package now ships a tmpfiles.d entry, so systemd creates /var/lib/orion-belt and /var/log/orion-belt at boot.

A host key that changed with every update​

On these systems a package's scripts run again for each new OS deployment, in a fresh copy of /etc. The SSH host key the package generated would have been replaced on every rpm-ostree upgrade, and agents and clients would have seen a different gateway key each time. There the package now leaves the key to the server, which creates it on first start in the live /etc, where it stays.

Installing​

sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/yum.repos.d/orion-belt.repo https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/orion-belt.repo
sudo rpm-ostree install orion-belt postgresql-server
sudo systemctl reboot

Then continue with Get started. Nothing changes on other distributions.

Also in 1.5.1​

Dependency updates, among them the gorilla/websocket fix for GO-2026-6278. The release notes list everything.

entry.title: Orion Belt v1.5 — SDKs, agent remote management and an AGPL license
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.5.0 adds Python and TypeScript SDKs for the whole API, remote management for agents, bulk grants, tunnels that survive network drops, standard API errors and the fixes from a security audit. It is now open source under the AGPL v3.0, with verifiable build provenance.
entry.content:
Orion Belt 1.5.0 makes the gateway easier to automate and easier to trust. It ships SDKs for every API endpoint, lets you manage agents from the gateway, and fixes everything a security audit found. It is also the first release under an open source license, and the first with build provenance you can check.

Python and TypeScript SDKs​

pip install orion-belt-sdk and npm install @orion-belt/sdk give you a client for every /api/v1 endpoint, with no runtime dependencies. CI checks both against the server's route table, so a new endpoint can't ship without them. See SDKs and the SDK post.

Agent remote management​

oadmin agents reload, drain, undrain and update run over the connection the agent already holds open to the gateway. No SSH to the host, no inbound port. Each command is admin or operator only and audited. See Agent remote management.

Bulk grants and effective access​

One call grants or revokes an access type for every user × machine pair, up to 500, each applied and audited on its own. The console gains multi-select, an effective access view and server-side search. See Permissions.

Tunnels that survive network drops​

Agents redial as soon as a link drops, with jittered backoff. The gateway pings agents and clients every 15 seconds, so dead links are noticed quickly, and a reconnecting agent is no longer shown as offline.

Standard API errors​

Every error now has a code: invalid, unauthenticated, forbidden, not_found, conflict, unavailable or internal, each with a fixed HTTP status. Internal details never reach a 500 response. See API errors.

Security audit fixes​

An external audit in early November found four issues; all are fixed, along with what we found while fixing them:

  • Generated agent install scripts and install-server.sh verify every download against the signed checksums.txt.
  • Deleting a machine keeps its recordings until the retention sweep. Agent registration, credential changes and file browser actions are audited. MFA backup codes can no longer be reused.
  • The API server has timeouts, a request body limit and security headers.
  • With a Host CA configured, agents no longer trust a gateway that omits its certificate.
  • The server container runs as orionbelt, not root.

Now AGPL v3.0​

Orion Belt is now open source under the GNU AGPL v3.0, replacing Apache 2.0 with the Commons Clause. Using, modifying and running it stays free, including commercially. What changes and why.

Verifiable releases​

Every release file and container image comes with SLSA level 3 provenance and a GitHub attestation, alongside the GPG signatures. You can check that a binary was built by the release workflow from the v1.5.0 tag. See Verify a release and the post on how we build releases.

Upgrade notes​

  • JWT secret: the server refuses to start with the example placeholder secret or one shorter than 32 bytes. Package installs and upgrades replace the placeholder with a random secret, which signs everyone out once. For Docker or hand-written configs, set one with openssl rand -hex 32.
  • Database migration: the first start converts timestamp columns to TIMESTAMPTZ, rewriting each table once under a lock. Expect a pause on a large audit_logs. A non-UTC host whose time zone can't be detected needs ORION_DB_LEGACY_TIMEZONE.
  • Unsigned builds: generated install scripts need signed release packages. For a local dist/, tick "Allow an unsigned local build".
  • Alpine: the chown step from the 1.4.0 install guide is no longer needed; the package owns its directories correctly.

Full notes are on the v1.5.0 release.

entry.title: Orion Belt is now open source under the AGPL v3.0
entry.summary: From 1.5.0, Orion Belt is licensed under the GNU AGPL v3.0 only, replacing Apache 2.0 with the Commons Clause. What you can do, what you must share, and what it means for the SDKs.
entry.content:
From 1.5.0, Orion Belt is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 only (AGPL-3.0-only). It replaces Apache 2.0 with the Commons Clause, which we used from the first release. Orion Belt is now open source in the OSI sense, not only source-available.

What you can do​

  • Run Orion Belt for any purpose, including inside a company and for paying customers' infrastructure.
  • Read, audit and modify the code.
  • Package it, mirror it and redistribute it.

There is no fee and no "internal use only" condition. The Commons Clause restriction on selling Orion Belt is gone.

What you must do in return​

The AGPL asks for one thing: if you pass the software on, you pass on the source too.

  • Distributing it (a modified binary, an appliance, an image you hand to others): ship the corresponding source under the AGPL.
  • Offering a modified version over a network (users connect to your changed gateway): offer those users the source of your version.

Running an unmodified Orion Belt triggers neither. Your configuration, your scripts and the machines behind the gateway are not covered by the license. This is a summary, not legal advice; the LICENSE text is what applies.

Why we changed​

When we explained the Commons Clause, we named three goals: keep the code auditable, keep self-hosting free, and stop a vendor from wrapping the project as a closed hosted service. The AGPL meets all three. Anyone can run a hosted Orion Belt, but they have to publish the changes they make to it, which is the protection we were after.

What the Commons Clause added on top was a ban on selling, and that came at a cost. It is not an OSI license, so teams with an "OSI-approved only" policy could not adopt Orion Belt at all, and packagers and security reviewers had to read a custom clause before they could even evaluate it. The AGPL is a license those teams already have a policy for.

The SDKs​

The Python and TypeScript SDKs are AGPL too. An application that bundles an SDK and is distributed, or served to others over a network, should be under an AGPL-compatible license. Calling the REST API directly, with any HTTP client, does not bring the AGPL into your code.

The SDK packages on PyPI and npm still carry the old license metadata from their 1.0.0 release. Their next release picks up the AGPL.

Older releases​

Releases up to and including 1.4.x stay under the license they shipped with. A license doesn't change retroactively. Upgrade to 1.5.0 to run under the AGPL.

Related​

  • Orion Belt v1.5
  • Apache 2.0 + Commons Clause, before 1.5.0
  • Open-source PAM landscape

entry.title: How to check that an Orion Belt binary is the one we built
entry.summary: From 1.5.0, every Orion Belt release file and container image has SLSA level 3 provenance and a GitHub attestation next to its GPG signature. What each proof tells you, how to check it, and the rest of the supply-chain work behind it.
entry.content:
An access gateway holds the keys to every machine behind it, so the binary you run matters as much as the code you read. From 1.5.0, each Orion Belt release lets you check not only who signed a file, but how and from what it was built.

Three proofs, three questions​

ProofQuestion it answers
GPG signature (<file>.sig, checksums.txt.sig)Was this file signed with the Orion Belt release key?
SLSA provenance (orion-belt-v1.5.0.intoto.jsonl)Was it built by our release workflow, from the v1.5.0 tag of our repository?
GitHub attestationThe same, recorded by GitHub, for release files and both container images

The GPG key signs every release file and the package repositories. It proves a file came from someone with the key. It can't tell you what was built: a signed binary built from a modified tree would pass.

Provenance closes that gap. The release workflow records which repository, commit and workflow produced each file, and that statement is signed with a short-lived certificate issued to the workflow run itself. No maintainer holds a key that could sign a false one.

Checking a file​

TAG=v1.5.0
FILE=orion-belt_1.5.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
gh release download "$TAG" -R orion-belt-dev/orion-belt \
  -p "$FILE" -p "orion-belt-$TAG.intoto.jsonl"

slsa-verifier verify-artifact "$FILE" \
  --provenance-path "orion-belt-$TAG.intoto.jsonl" \
  --source-uri github.com/orion-belt-dev/orion-belt \
  --source-tag "$TAG"

gh attestation verify "$FILE" --repo orion-belt-dev/orion-belt

And an image:

gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/orion-belt-dev/orion-belt-server:1.5.0 \
  --repo orion-belt-dev/orion-belt

The images also carry BuildKit provenance and an SBOM. The full walkthrough, including GPG, is in Verify a release.

If you install from pkgs.orion-belt.dev, your package manager already checks the GPG signature on every package.

Why only from 1.5.0​

Provenance has to be produced at build time. We could generate statements for 1.4.0 and earlier now, but they would describe builds that never happened that way. Older releases keep their GPG signatures and nothing more.

The rest of the work​

Provenance was the visible part of a wider pass over how the project is built and maintained:

  • Every GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA (except the SLSA generator, which has to be referenced by its release tag for slsa-verifier to trust it). Container base images in the lab are pinned by digest, and workflow tokens get write access only in the jobs that need it.
  • master needs two approving reviews, a fresh approval after the last push, and nine passing CI checks, including a gate that fails on any known vulnerability in a dependency.
  • Go fuzz targets cover scope parsing, SCP file names, shell word splitting and password hash verification. The last one found a panic on malformed stored hashes, fixed in 1.5.0.
  • A security policy with private reporting through GitHub advisories or maintainers@orion-belt.dev.

The project's OpenSSF Scorecard went from 7.1 to 9.4, and it holds the OpenSSF Best Practices passing badge. Scores aren't security, but they are a public checklist anyone can re-run against us.

Related​

  • Orion Belt v1.5
  • Linux packages and labs

entry.title: Automating Orion Belt from Python and TypeScript
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.5.0 ships Python and TypeScript SDKs that cover every API endpoint, with no runtime dependencies. How they stay complete, how to log in with an SSH key, and a JIT access script to start from.
entry.content:
Most of what people build around a PAM gateway is glue: a chat bot that files access requests, a nightly job that reviews standing grants, a deploy pipeline that asks for an hour on production. With 1.5.0, that glue can be written against a typed client in Python or TypeScript instead of hand-rolled HTTP calls.

pip install orion-belt-sdk        # Python 3.11+
npm install @orion-belt/sdk       # Node 20+, Deno, Bun, browsers

Complete by construction​

An SDK that covers "the main endpoints" quietly falls behind. These two cover every /api/v1 route, and they stay that way because the build says so.

The server's routes are generated from the Go router into sdk/routes.json. A server test fails if the router and the file disagree, and each SDK has a contract test that fails if a route has no method. Adding an endpoint without adding it to both clients turns CI red.

Both clients follow the Go SDK's method names (list_machines in Python, listMachines in TypeScript), so code ports between the three with little thought.

No dependencies​

The Python client uses only the standard library. The TypeScript client uses the platform fetch. Neither pulls anything into your dependency tree, which matters for a tool that holds admin credentials to your access gateway.

Log in with an SSH key​

Scripts don't need a stored password. Prove you hold a key registered to the user, and the client keeps the API key it gets back:

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
from orion_belt_sdk import OrionBeltClient

key = serialization.load_ssh_private_key(open("id_ed25519", "rb").read(), password=None)


class Signer:
    public_key = key.public_key().public_bytes(
        serialization.Encoding.OpenSSH, serialization.PublicFormat.OpenSSH
    ).decode()

    def sign(self, data: bytes) -> tuple[str, bytes]:
        return "ssh-ed25519", key.sign(data)


client = OrionBeltClient("https://orion.example.com")
client.login_with_ssh_key("deploy-bot", Signer())

cryptography is only needed for this example; the SDK itself doesn't require it. Password and TOTP login, session tokens and JWTs work too. See SDKs.

Example: ask for an hour on a machine​

A deploy job that requests just-in-time access, then waits for a human to approve it:

import { OrionBeltClient } from '@orion-belt/sdk';

const client = new OrionBeltClient({
  baseUrl: 'https://orion.example.com',
  apiKey: process.env.ORION_API_KEY,
});

const machine = await client.getMachineByName('web-01');

const request = await client.createAccessRequest({
  machine_id: machine.id,
  reason: `deploy ${process.env.GIT_SHA}`,
  duration: 3600,
  remote_users: ['deploy'],
});

console.log(`Access request ${request.id} is waiting for approval`);

The approver sees the request, its reason and its risk signals in the console or in chat, and the access expires on its own an hour later.

License​

The SDKs are AGPL v3.0, like the rest of Orion Belt. If you bundle one into an application you distribute or serve to others, check that your license is compatible. More on the license change.

Related​

  • SDK reference
  • JIT access approvals
  • Orion Belt v1.5

entry.title: Secure RDP access without exposing port 3389 — VPN, RD Gateway and reverse tunnels compared
entry.summary: Exposing RDP on port 3389 to the internet invites brute force and exploits. Compare the alternatives — VPN, Microsoft RD Gateway, SSH tunnels and an outbound reverse tunnel — and see how Orion Belt 1.4 brokers RDP and VNC with approvals and audit, without inbound ports.
entry.content:
The safest way to offer RDP is to not listen for it on the internet at all. An RDP port open to the world gets scanned and brute-forced continuously, and RDP has had remote code execution bugs severe enough to be wormable (BlueKeep, CVE-2019-0708). This post compares the common ways to put something in front of RDP and VNC, and where Orion Belt 1.4 fits.

The options​

ApproachInbound port on the target networkPer-machine accessApproval / time limitAudit of who connected
RDP open to the internet3389 on every hostWindows login onlyNoWindows event log
VPN, then RDPVPN portNetwork-wideNoVPN logs + event log
Microsoft RD Gateway443 on the gatewayResource policiesNoGateway logs
SSH tunnel through a bastion22 on the bastionWhat the bastion allowsNoBastion logs
Outbound reverse tunnel (Orion Belt)NoneGrant per machineYesGateway audit log

VPN​

Puts users on the network, then they RDP directly. Simple, but access is network-wide: anyone on the VPN can try RDP against anything they can route to. Fine for small teams; weak least privilege.

RD Gateway​

Microsoft's Remote Desktop Gateway wraps RDP in HTTPS and applies connection and resource authorization policies. It's the standard choice in Windows-centric shops. It still needs an inbound HTTPS endpoint, a Windows Server to run it, and has no request-and-approve flow.

SSH tunnel through a bastion​

ssh -L 13389:win-01:3389 bastion works anywhere OpenSSH does. The bastion needs to reach the Windows host, and nothing records who opened which tunnel beyond sshd logs.

Outbound reverse tunnel​

An agent on the target network dials out to a gateway. Users connect to the gateway, which checks their grant and relays the stream through the agent's existing connection. The target network opens no inbound port at all.

How it works in Orion Belt 1.4​

RDP and VNC are access types of their own, rdp and vnc. A grant for one covers that protocol only, and like SSH access it can be requested just in time:

osh rdp win-01 -r --reason "patch Tuesday" -d 1800   # request, wait for approval
osh rdp win-01                                       # prints e.g. 127.0.0.1:53211

Point mstsc, Remmina, FreeRDP or any VNC viewer at the printed address. Plain OpenSSH works too:

ssh -N -L 13389:win-01:3389 alice@orion-gateway.example.com

The agent decides where traffic goes. By default it relays RDP to 127.0.0.1:3389 and VNC to 127.0.0.1:5900 on its own host. Its config can point a protocol at another address on its network, or turn it off:

agent:
  name: win-01
  tunnels:
    rdp: 10.0.4.20:3389   # a Windows desktop next to the agent
    vnc: "off"

The gateway only names the protocol, so it can never steer an agent at an address its config doesn't list.

Windows hosts today: the agent doesn't build for Windows yet. Run it on a Linux machine on the same network and point tunnels.rdp at the Windows host.

What gets audited​

Each connection writes tunnel.open and tunnel.close entries (protocol, machine, bytes each way, duration); refused attempts write tunnel.denied. They appear in the compliance reports as rdp_session and vnc_session rows.

RDP and VNC sessions are not recorded yet. The stream is encrypted end to end between your client and the target; recording it would need the gateway to terminate the protocol. Keep that in mind if screen recording is a hard requirement.

Hardening RDP itself​

Whatever is in front, keep these on:

  • Network Level Authentication (NLA), so authentication happens before a full session is set up.
  • Account lockout for repeated failures.
  • Firewall rules that accept 3389 only from the relay (here, the agent's host, or 127.0.0.1 when the agent runs on the target).
  • Patching on the RDP stack.

FAQ​

Is it safe to expose RDP to the internet? No. Put a gateway, VPN or tunnel in front and accept RDP only from it.

Can I use RDP through an SSH tunnel? Yes: forward a local port to the host's 3389 through an SSH server that can reach it. Orion Belt accepts exactly that with plain ssh -L, and checks the user's rdp grant first.

Does this work for VNC? Yes, the same way, on port 5900 with the vnc access type.

Related​

  • Orion Belt v1.4
  • RDP and VNC guide
  • Why reverse SSH agents

entry.title: How to give engineers temporary Kubernetes access with expiring RoleBindings
entry.summary: A step-by-step guide to just-in-time Kubernetes access — why standing kubeconfigs are a risk, how expiring RoleBindings and impersonation work, and how Orion Belt 1.4 issues, reconciles and removes them through an in-cluster agent with no exposed API server.
entry.content:
Temporary Kubernetes access means a user gets a RoleBinding for a specific namespace and role, for a fixed time, and the binding is deleted when that time is up. Kubernetes RBAC has no expiry field, so something outside the cluster has to create and remove those bindings reliably. This guide shows the pattern and how Orion Belt 1.4 does it.

Why standing kubeconfigs are a problem​

The usual setup: every engineer has a kubeconfig with a long-lived credential bound to a broad role, often cluster-admin "temporarily".

  • Kubeconfigs get copied: into CI variables, laptops, chat messages.
  • Bindings outlive their reason. A role granted for an incident stays.
  • Revoking is manual, and depends on someone remembering.
  • The API server is reachable from wherever those laptops are.

Kubernetes' own RBAC good practices recommend least privilege and minimal use of cluster-admin. Expiring access is how you get there without slowing people down.

The pattern​

  1. A user requests a role in a namespace (payments/edit) with a reason and a duration.
  2. Someone approves.
  3. A controller creates a RoleBinding for that user, labelled with its expiry.
  4. kubectl traffic reaches the API server as that user, so RBAC enforces exactly the binding.
  5. When the time is up, the binding is deleted, even if the system that granted it is down.

Steps 4 and 5 are where home-grown versions usually fall short.

How Orion Belt does it​

Grants have access type k8s and scopes of the form namespace/role. payments/edit binds the edit ClusterRole in payments as a RoleBinding; */view binds view cluster-wide as a ClusterRoleBinding.

Subjects are Kubernetes users named orion:<username>, so a binding issued by Orion Belt can never match an identity from another authenticator.

An agent runs inside the cluster and dials out to the gateway, like the agents on hosts. The API server is never exposed.

kubectl goes through osh kube. The agent forwards requests to the API server with its service account and Impersonate-User: orion:<user>, after stripping any credentials or impersonation headers the client sent. RBAC then allows exactly what the issued bindings allow (user impersonation).

Reconciling keeps the cluster matched to the grants. The gateway compares the bindings it manages (named orion-*, labelled app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=orion-belt) with active grants and creates, updates or deletes to match: when a grant changes, when the agent connects, and every 30 seconds.

The agent enforces expiry on its own. It deletes expired bindings every minute, even while the gateway is unreachable.

Step by step​

1. Install the in-cluster agent. Register a machine for the cluster in the console (its name is the cluster's name in grants), then:

kubectl create namespace orion-belt
kubectl -n orion-belt create secret generic orion-belt-agent-key \
  --from-file=agent_key=./agent-key
kubectl apply -f orion-belt-agent.yaml   # from deploy/kubernetes/, with server and agent name set

The manifest's ClusterRole lets the agent manage bindings, bind ClusterRoles and impersonate users. Narrow bind with resourceNames to the roles you allow (for example view, edit).

2. Request access.

osh kube prod-eu -r --scope payments/edit --reason "INC-42" -d 1800
# Kubernetes API of prod-eu relayed on 127.0.0.1:53817
# export KUBECONFIG=/home/alice/.orion-belt/kube/prod-eu.yaml

3. Use kubectl normally.

kubectl get pods             # namespace defaults to the first scope's
kubectl -n default get pods  # Forbidden: outside the grant

The generated kubeconfig holds no credentials. It points at a loopback relay, and the gateway authenticates the SSH connection behind it.

4. Check for drift.

oadmin machines kube-reconcile prod-eu          # report only
oadmin machines kube-reconcile prod-eu --apply  # fix now

Audit trail​

Every step is logged: the request and approval (access_type: k8s with its scopes), each binding created, updated or deleted with the reason (granted, expired, revoked, orphaned), and each kubectl relay connection. The compliance reports list them as k8s_session rows.

FAQ​

Can a Kubernetes RoleBinding expire on its own? No. RBAC objects have no expiry. A controller has to delete them; Orion Belt does it from both the gateway and the in-cluster agent.

Does this work with managed clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS)? The agent only uses standard Kubernetes RBAC and impersonation through its own service account, nothing provider-specific, and needs outbound access to the gateway. Our end-to-end tests run on kind; tell us how it goes on a managed cluster.

Does the user need a kubeconfig from the cloud provider? No. osh kube writes one that points at the local relay.

Related​

  • Orion Belt v1.4
  • Kubernetes guide
  • What is privileged access management?

entry.title: Orion Belt v1.4 — RDP, VNC and just-in-time Kubernetes access
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.4.0 adds RDP and VNC through the reverse agent tunnel, just-in-time Kubernetes RoleBindings through an in-cluster agent, compliance reports, and risk signals with access explain and anomaly flags.
entry.content:
Orion Belt 1.4.0 takes the outbound-agent model beyond SSH. RDP, VNC and kubectl now go through the same agents that dial out to the gateway, with the same request, approve and expire flow and the same audit trail.

RDP and VNC​

osh rdp win-01 and osh vnc lab-02 open a local port relayed to the machine through its agent; point any RDP or VNC client at it. Plain ssh -N -L 13389:win-01:3389 alice@gateway works too. Grants use the new rdp and vnc access types, and the agent decides where each protocol goes, so the gateway can never steer it at an arbitrary host. See RDP and VNC.

Just-in-time Kubernetes access​

An approved k8s grant, scoped as payments/edit or */view, becomes a real RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding for orion:<user>, issued by an agent running inside the cluster. osh kube prod-eu writes a credential-free kubeconfig and relays kubectl as that user, so Kubernetes RBAC enforces exactly the grant. Bindings are reconciled against grants continuously, survive gateway restarts, and are deleted by the agent itself when they expire, even if the gateway is unreachable. See Kubernetes.

Compliance and access intelligence​

  • Compliance reports: SOC 2 access, ISO 27001 access review and PCI admin activity, as CSV, PDF or JSON. They include RDP, VNC and kubectl connections.
  • Risk signals, access explain and anomaly flags: every request records who, from where and how; a risk policy can escalate or auto-approve; osh explain says why access is allowed or denied; and unusual sessions are flagged for review.

Upgrade notes​

  • both grants now cover ssh and scp only. Before 1.4.0 the permission check matched both for any access type; with tunnel and Kubernetes types added, that would have widened every existing SSH grant.
  • Agents must be on 1.4.0 for RDP, VNC and Kubernetes. Older agents keep working for SSH and are told to upgrade if a tunnel is requested.

Full notes are on the v1.4.0 release.

entry.title: Orion Belt 1.3 — signed packages for every Linux distribution, clients for every OS
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.3 publishes signed apt, dnf, zypper, apk and pacman repositories at pkgs.orion-belt.dev across nine CPU architectures, clients for macOS, Windows and the BSDs, a one-line installer, an access capability catalog in the console, and gateway hardening.
entry.content:
Orion Belt 1.3.0 (October 22, with 1.3.1 the next day) makes installing the gateway, the agent and the clients a package manager command on almost any machine. Everything comes from signed repositories at pkgs.orion-belt.dev, so upgrades arrive with the rest of your system updates.

Install in one line​

curl -fsSL https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/install.sh | sh                # clients: osh, ocp, oadmin
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- agent    # agent (Linux)
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- server   # server (Linux)
irm https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/install.ps1 | iex                     # clients on Windows

On Linux the script adds the repository for your package manager and installs from it. Every download is checked against the release's checksums.txt, and its GPG signature is checked when gpg is installed. If you'd rather not pipe to a shell, add the repository by hand; the Get started guide has the commands per OS.

What's covered​

PlatformPackage formatArchitectures
Debian, Ubuntu, Raspberry Pi OS.deb (apt)amd64, arm64, armhf, armel, i386, ppc64el, s390x, riscv64, loong64
Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma, Amazon Linux.rpm (dnf/yum)x86_64, aarch64, armv7hl, armv6hl, i386, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64, loongarch64
openSUSE, SLES.rpm (zypper)as above
Alpine.apkx86_64, aarch64, armv7, armhf, x86, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64, loongarch64
Arch Linux, Arch Linux ARM, Arch Linux 32pacmanx86_64, aarch64, armv7h, i686
macOSarchiveamd64, arm64 (clients)
Windowszip, scoopamd64, arm64, 386 (clients)
FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, illumos, Solarisarchiveclients
Containers (GHCR)imageamd64, arm64, arm/v7, arm/v6, 386, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64

Three packages per Linux platform: orion-belt (gateway), orion-belt-agent and orion-belt-tools (osh, ocp, oadmin). The server and agent packages work with systemd, OpenRC, runit and SysV init.

Why so many architectures​

Agents run where your machines are, and that's not only x86 servers: Raspberry Pis in a lab, ARM boards at the edge, s390x and ppc64le in older data centers. The agent is a single Go binary with no runtime dependencies, so building it for nine CPUs costs CI minutes, not maintenance.

Signed end to end​

  • The apt, dnf, zypper and pacman repositories are signed with the release GPG key.
  • .deb files carry an embedded signature and .rpm files a native one.
  • Every release file has a detached .sig, and checksums.txt is signed.

The key fingerprint is on the front page of pkgs.orion-belt.dev; compare it before you trust the repository.

Also in 1.3​

  • Capability catalog in the console (#57), building on the access catalog from 1.2.1: users see what they can request.
  • CLI coverage for the endpoints added since 1.0 (#64).
  • Gateway hardening: plugin settings validate admin-set URLs, paths and mail headers; Slack response_url posts are restricted; users can only delete their own SSH keys.
  • Exec fixes: one-shot commands (ssh user+web-01@gateway uptime) run on the machine named in the SSH username, no longer lose output, and no longer hang when the command fails. A shell's last output arrives before the session ends.

FAQ​

Is there an apt repository for Orion Belt? Yes: deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/orion-belt.gpg] https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev stable main, after downloading the key from https://pkgs.orion-belt.dev/orion-belt.gpg.

Does the agent run on a Raspberry Pi? Yes. The armhf build runs on Raspberry Pi OS, and arm64 on 64-bit Pi OS.

Can I run the gateway in Docker instead? Yes. Server and agent images are on GHCR for eight architectures.

Release notes: v1.3.0 · v1.3.1

entry.title: SSH key management at scale — authorized_keys sprawl, certificates and gateways compared
entry.summary: Three ways to manage SSH access across a fleet — distributing authorized_keys, SSH certificates from a CA, and an access gateway — with how each handles onboarding, offboarding, rotation and audit, and when to combine them.
entry.content:
SSH key sprawl is what happens when every person's public key is copied into authorized_keys on every server they ever needed. Nobody knows which keys are still in use, offboarding means editing hundreds of files, and a key from a laptop retired three years ago still opens production. There are three ways out. This post compares them.

The three models​

authorized_keys distributionSSH certificates (CA)Access gateway
Where trust livesEach host's key filesThe CA public key on each hostThe gateway
OnboardingPush key to N hostsIssue a certificateCreate user + grant
OffboardingRemove key from N hostsStop issuing; old certs expireDisable user; access ends now
Credential lifetimeForeverHours, by designSession; grants can expire
Per-machine accessWhich hosts got the keyPrincipals in the certGrants per machine
Approval workflowNoneNone built inBuilt in
Session recordingNoNoYes
Host changes neededEvery changeOnce (TrustedUserCAKeys)Agent install, once

Model 1: distributing authorized_keys​

Config management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef) pushes keys to hosts. It works, and most teams start here.

It breaks down on three things:

  • Offboarding is a deploy. Until the run reaches every host, the key still works. Hosts that miss the run keep it.
  • Keys never expire. OpenSSH supports an expiry-time option in authorized_keys, but almost nobody uses it.
  • No record of use. You know who could log in, not who did.

If you stay here, at least set LogLevel VERBOSE in sshd so logins record the key fingerprint, and audit keys against your directory regularly.

Model 2: SSH certificates​

OpenSSH has supported certificates since 5.4. A CA signs a user's public key with a validity window and a list of principals (the accounts it may log in as). Hosts trust the CA, not individual keys (ssh-keygen(1) CERTIFICATES).

# On each host, once:
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/user_ca.pub

# Issuing a cert valid for 8 hours, as user "deploy":
ssh-keygen -s user_ca -I alice@example.com -n deploy -V +8h id_ed25519.pub

Certificates fix expiry and offboarding: stop issuing and access ends when the last certificate runs out. Host certificates fix the other direction, replacing "trust on first use" with a CA-signed host key.

What they don't give you: an approval step, a record of the session, or per-request scoping, unless you build the issuing service yourself. The CA key also becomes the most sensitive secret you own.

Model 3: an access gateway​

Users authenticate to a gateway; the gateway decides per request whether they may reach a machine as a given account, then brokers the session. Users' keys never need to be on the targets.

With Orion Belt:

  • Users register their own keys with the gateway (osh keys add), and remove them the same way.
  • Grants are per user, machine and remote user. Privileged ones are requested just in time and expire.
  • Every session is recorded at the gateway.
  • Targets run an agent that dials out; you don't manage keys on them at all.

Combining them​

The models stack well. Orion Belt includes an optional SSH CA: it issues short-lived user certificates for operators and host certificates for the gateway and agents. That gives you short-lived credentials (model 2) behind a gateway with grants, approvals and recording (model 3). Static authorized_keys remain only for break-glass.

A migration path​

  1. Turn on LogLevel VERBOSE and find out which keys are actually used.
  2. Put a gateway in front of production and move people to it.
  3. Turn on short-lived certificates.
  4. Remove personal keys from authorized_keys on targets, host group by host group, keeping one documented break-glass key.

FAQ​

How do I revoke an SSH key on all servers at once? With authorized_keys, you can't, only push a change and wait. With certificates, use a revocation list (RevokedKeys) or wait for expiry. With a gateway, disable the user or remove the key at the gateway, and it takes effect on the next connection.

How often should SSH keys be rotated? Rotation matters less when credentials are short-lived. With certificates valid for hours, the user key itself can stay put; protect it with a hardware token instead.

Are SSH certificates better than keys? Certificates are keys plus a signature with an expiry and principals. They fix expiry and offboarding; they don't add approvals or recording.

Related​

  • SSH bastion host best practices
  • MFA and WebAuthn for SSH

entry.title: Self-service SSH access requests — let engineers see what they can ask for
entry.summary: Just-in-time access only works if people know what to request. Orion Belt 1.2.1 adds an access catalog that shows each user what they can request, plus authentication and proxy hardening and a terminal resize fix.
entry.content:
Just-in-time access fails quietly when engineers don't know what to ask for. They guess machine names, request too broadly "to be safe", or ping an admin on chat, which is the workflow JIT was supposed to replace. Orion Belt 1.2.1, released September 29, adds an access catalog to fix that.

The access catalog​

The console now shows each user the capabilities they could request, based on their current relationships: which machines, as which remote users, with which access types. Instead of typing web-03 and hoping, they pick from a list that only contains things an approver could actually grant them.

That has a few effects:

  • Fewer rejected requests. Requests for machines a user has no path to don't get filed.
  • Narrower requests. When the exact option is visible, people stop asking for more than they need.
  • No information leak. The catalog is computed per user, from the same relationships the authorization check uses (ReBAC), so it doesn't reveal machines a user has no business knowing about.

How a request flows​

  1. The engineer picks a target from the catalog, adds a reason and a duration, and submits. Or from the CLI: osh --request-access deploy@web-03 --reason "INC-1234" --duration 1800, then osh requests list to follow it.
  2. Approvers are notified in the console bell and, with the chat plugins, in Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams or Rocket.Chat, where they can approve in place.
  3. On approval the grant is active for the requested duration, then expires without anyone revoking it.
  4. The session is recorded and tied to the request in the audit log.

Detail on the approval side: JIT access approvals.

Also in 1.2.1​

  • Authentication, authorization and proxy hardening across the gateway (PR #99).
  • Terminal resize fix: window size changes now reach the target's PTY, so full-screen programs (htop, vim, less) redraw correctly when you resize your terminal (#103).
  • Tracing fix: the OTLP/HTTP traces path is set explicitly, so HTTP collectors receive spans (PR #101).
  • Dependency updates, including gRPC and the OpenTelemetry SDK.

Designing a request policy that people follow​

A catalog helps; the policy around it matters more.

DecisionSuggested default
What needs a requestProduction and anything holding customer data
What stays standingDev and staging, for the team that owns them
Default duration1 hour; 8 hours maximum without a second approver
Reason fieldRequired; link a ticket or incident
ApproversNot the requester; two people for the most sensitive systems

Keep the request faster than the workaround. If requesting access takes longer than finding a shared key in someone's dotfiles, people will find the key.

FAQ​

What is a self-service access request? A request a user files themselves for specific, time-limited access, which an approver accepts or rejects, instead of asking an admin to change permissions by hand.

Can approvals happen in Slack? Yes. The chat plugins post requests to Slack, Discord, Teams or Rocket.Chat with approve and reject actions.

Release notes: v1.2.1

entry.title: Tracing SSH sessions with OpenTelemetry — finding the slow hop
entry.summary: How Orion Belt traces an SSH session across the gateway, the agent and the target with OpenTelemetry — the span tree, how W3C trace context crosses an SSH channel, what is kept out of spans, and how to turn it on.
entry.content:
When an SSH login through a gateway takes eight seconds, the question is which hop is slow: authorization, the gateway → agent tunnel, or the agent → target connection. Logs and metrics don't answer that well. Distributed tracing does. Since 1.1.0, Orion Belt emits OpenTelemetry traces for SSH sessions across both processes.

Metrics, logs or traces?​

QuestionUse
Is it up? How many sessions? Alert meMetrics (/metrics, Prometheus)
What exactly happened in this session?Logs and the session recording
Which hop is slow or failing?Traces

The span tree​

One trace per SSH session, spanning the gateway and the agent:

gateway.ssh.session                (gateway, SERVER)
├── gateway.authorize              machine lookup + permission check
├── gateway.agent.open_channel     the gateway → agent hop (CLIENT)
│   └── agent.session              (agent, SERVER, same trace)
│       └── agent.target.shell     the agent → target hop
│           or agent.target.exec   one-shot command / scp
└── gateway.proxy.shell            session body
    or gateway.proxy.exec

Connect latency shows up in gateway.authorize and gateway.agent.open_channel. The proxy.* and target.shell spans last as long as the user stays connected: read them as session duration, not latency.

Attributes to filter on: orion.user, orion.target.machine, orion.target.remote_user, and orion.session.id, which joins a trace to the session recording and the audit log.

Carrying trace context through SSH​

HTTP has headers for W3C trace context. SSH doesn't. The gateway puts the traceparent into the extra data of the SSH channel-open request it sends to the agent, and the agent parents its spans on it.

This is tolerant in both directions. An agent that predates tracing ignores the extra data. A new agent that receives none starts its own trace and marks it with orion.trace.linked_to_gateway=false. A trace-context problem never fails a session, so you can upgrade gateway and agents separately. That attribute is also how you spot a half-upgraded fleet.

What stays out of spans​

Spans go to a collector, which usually has weaker access controls than session recordings. So commands are recorded as the program name only (orion.command), never with arguments or NAME=value environment prefixes. A mysql -p... typed by an admin doesn't end up in your tracing backend.

Turning it on​

Both sides read the same block. You need both for a full trace.

# server.yaml and agent.yaml
tracing:
  enabled: true
  endpoint: "otel-collector:4317"   # gRPC wants host:port, not a URL
  protocol: grpc                    # or http
  insecure: false                   # true only for a trusted plaintext link
  sample_ratio: 1.0

Leave endpoint empty to use the standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* environment variables instead. Any OTLP backend works: the OpenTelemetry Collector, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb.

Service names default to orion-belt-gateway and orion-belt-agent-<agent name>. The agent name is included on purpose: a fleet that all reports as one service makes the agent hop useless to look at.

What it costs​

Disabled means free: no exporter, no tracer provider, one atomic load per entry point. Measured with the project's benchmarks on an M1:

PathDisabledEnabled
Start + End a span2.3 ns, 0 allocs644 ns, 3 allocs

A test in CI asserts the disabled path doesn't allocate.

Not traced (yet)​

The HTTP API isn't instrumented; API requests carry a request_id for log correlation instead. Web terminal sessions get the agent hop but no HTTP parent span.

FAQ​

Can OpenTelemetry trace an SSH connection? Not out of the box: SSH has no header for trace context. A gateway that controls both ends can carry it, as Orion Belt does in the channel-open data.

Does tracing record what users type? No. Spans hold timing, identities and the program name. Keystrokes and output are in the session recording, which has its own access controls.

Related​

  • Orion Belt 1.1 and 1.2
  • Why reverse SSH agents

entry.title: What is privileged access management (PAM)? A plain-English guide for infrastructure teams
entry.summary: Privileged access management (PAM) controls, approves, records and expires access to the accounts and systems that can do the most damage. What PAM covers, the terms (PASM, PEDM, JIT, standing privilege), and how it applies to SSH.
entry.content:
Privileged access management (PAM) is the set of controls that decides who may use powerful accounts and systems, when, with whose approval, and keeps a record of what they did. "Privileged" means access that can change production, read sensitive data or turn off other controls: root on a server, a database admin login, a cloud admin role.

PAM is not to be confused with Linux PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules), the library that handles logins on a Linux host. Same acronym, different thing.

What PAM does​

CapabilityQuestion it answers
Access controlWho may reach which system, as which account?
ApprovalDid someone else agree before access was granted?
Time limitsWhen does the access end?
Credential protectionDoes the person ever see the password or key?
Session recordingWhat exactly happened during the session?
AuditCan we prove all of the above to an auditor later?

The vocabulary​

Standing privilege: access that is always on. A key in authorized_keys, an admin group membership. It's the default almost everywhere, and it's what attackers use after stealing a credential.

Just-in-time (JIT) access: access granted for a task and removed automatically afterwards. The goal is zero standing privilege: nobody holds production access until they need it. More on JIT approvals.

PASM, privileged account and session management: vaulting shared credentials, brokering sessions so the user never sees them, and recording those sessions.

PEDM, privilege elevation and delegation management: controlling what a user may do once logged in, such as sudo policies and endpoint elevation.

Break-glass access: an emergency path for when the normal one is down, used rarely and audited heavily.

Least privilege: the principle behind all of it. Each person gets the minimum access needed, for the minimum time.

Why teams adopt PAM​

  • Stolen credentials are the common path in. The Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report has listed the use of stolen credentials among the top breach actions for years. Access that doesn't exist yet can't be stolen.
  • Auditors ask for it. SOC 2 (CC6.1 to CC6.3), ISO 27001 (Annex A access control) and PCI DSS (requirements 7, 8 and 10) all ask who has access to what, how it was approved and how it is logged.
  • People leave. Standing keys and group memberships survive offboarding far too often.

PAM for SSH specifically​

Most enterprise PAM suites started with Windows and vaulted passwords. For Linux fleets, the privileged path is SSH, and it needs:

  1. A single entry point (a gateway or bastion) instead of direct SSH to each host.
  2. Per-machine grants tied to a person, not a shared key.
  3. JIT requests for production, with approval in the console or chat.
  4. Session recording taken at the gateway, out of reach of root on the target.
  5. MFA at the gateway.
  6. Short-lived credentials (SSH certificates) instead of static keys.

Orion Belt is a self-hosted SSH gateway built around those six. Targets run an agent that dials out, so they need no inbound SSH port.

PAM vs. related tools​

ToolMain jobOverlap with PAM
Identity provider (IdP)Who you are; SSOFeeds PAM identities; doesn't grant server access
VPNNetwork reachabilityNone at the account level
Bastion / jump hostOne network entry pointThe path, without approvals or recording (comparison)
Secrets managerStoring credentials for appsOverlaps with PASM vaulting
PAMWho, when, approved by whom, recorded—

FAQ​

Is PAM only for large enterprises? No. The need starts when more than one person has production access. What changes with size is how much of it you automate.

What's the difference between PAM and IAM? IAM manages identities and their general access. PAM is the subset that governs the highest-risk access more strictly: approval, time limits and recording.

Does PAM replace sudo policies? No. PAM decides who gets onto the machine and as which account; sudo policies (PEDM) decide what that account may do there.

Related​

  • Open-source PAM and SSH bastion options compared
  • SSH bastion host best practices
  • ReBAC for SSH machines

entry.title: SSH bastion host best practices — a hardening checklist
entry.summary: A checklist for running an SSH bastion or jump host safely in 2026 — identity, keys, MFA, network exposure, least privilege, session recording, logging and break-glass — with OpenSSH settings and where a PAM gateway replaces manual work.
entry.content:
A bastion host is the single door into your servers, so it has to be the most locked-down machine you run. This checklist covers the controls that matter, in the order they usually go wrong, with the OpenSSH settings for a plain jump host and what a PAM gateway does for you.

1. One identity per person​

Shared accounts (ubuntu, admin, deploy) destroy attribution. Every person gets their own login on the bastion, even if they land on a shared account on the target.

  • Plain bastion: one Unix user per person, provisioned from your directory.
  • Gateway: users exist at the gateway; the target account (remote_user) is part of the grant. Orion Belt logs both who you are and which account you used.

2. Keys only, no passwords​

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

Prefer ed25519 keys. Hardware-backed keys (ed25519-sk, ecdsa-sk) keep the private key on a FIDO2 token, so a stolen laptop disk is not a stolen key.

3. Short-lived credentials beat key rotation​

Long-lived keys in authorized_keys outlive the people who own them. SSH certificates signed by a CA expire on their own. With OpenSSH, set TrustedUserCAKeys on the hosts and issue certificates with ssh-keygen -s ca -V +8h. Orion Belt can run that CA for you (optional SSH CA).

4. MFA at the door​

The bastion is where MFA belongs: one place to enforce it, rather than every host. Options: FIDO2 SSH keys (the touch is the second factor), TOTP through PAM, or a gateway that requires TOTP or WebAuthn for the console (MFA and WebAuthn).

5. Expose as little as possible​

  • Only the bastion accepts SSH from outside. Targets accept SSH only from the bastion's address, or not at all.
  • With a reverse-agent gateway, targets open no inbound port: the agent dials out (why). There is nothing to scan.
  • Disable features you don't use on the bastion itself:
AllowTcpForwarding no      # unless you rely on ProxyJump through it
X11Forwarding no
AllowAgentForwarding no
PermitTunnel no

Agent forwarding on a shared bastion lets anyone with root on it use your keys while you're connected. Use ProxyJump (ssh -J bastion target) instead: the connection to the target is end to end from your laptop.

6. Least privilege, and time-boxed​

Standing access to production is the norm and the problem. Grant access per machine, and for privileged access, for a limited time after approval. In NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the controls auditors map this to are AC-6 (least privilege) and AC-2 (account management).

In Orion Belt, grants are per user, machine and remote user, and just-in-time requests expire on their own.

7. Record sessions off the target​

Logs on the target can be edited by root on the target. Record at the bastion. On a plain jump host with ProxyJump you can't see inside the session (it's encrypted end to end), so recording needs a gateway that terminates SSH. See how to audit SSH access on Linux.

8. Ship logs, alert on the unusual​

Send bastion logs off the box as they're written: sshd at LogLevel VERBOSE (logs key fingerprints), the gateway's audit log, and metrics. Alert on logins outside working hours, new source addresses and failed MFA bursts.

9. Patch it first​

The bastion is internet-facing and holds the keys to everything. It goes first in every OpenSSH and kernel update cycle, not last.

10. Plan break-glass before you need it​

When the bastion or your identity provider is down, how do you get in? Write it down: a sealed local admin credential, who can use it, and how its use is audited and rotated afterwards.

Checklist​

  • One identity per person; no shared bastion logins
  • Keys only; root login off
  • Short-lived certificates or a gateway instead of static keys
  • MFA enforced at the bastion
  • Targets accept SSH only via the bastion (or open no port at all)
  • Agent forwarding off; ProxyJump for hops
  • Per-machine, time-boxed grants for privileged access
  • Sessions recorded off the target
  • Logs shipped off-host with alerts
  • Bastion patched first
  • Documented break-glass

FAQ​

Is a bastion host still needed with a VPN? A VPN gives network access; it doesn't decide which machine a person may log into, record the session or expire access. Many teams run both.

ProxyJump or agent forwarding? ProxyJump. Agent forwarding exposes your agent to anyone with root on the bastion for as long as you're connected.

What's the difference between a bastion and PAM? A bastion controls the network path. PAM adds who may access what, when, with whose approval, and a record of it. More in SSH bastion vs PAM.

entry.title: Orion Belt 1.1 and 1.2 — tracing, report exports, usage analytics and a one-line installer
entry.summary: Orion Belt 1.1.0 adds OpenTelemetry tracing across the gateway and agent, PDF/CSV/SIEM report exports, a usage analytics dashboard, an org-wide notification policy and a Go SDK. 1.2.0 adds a one-line server installer and in-app notifications.
entry.content:
Two releases landed two weeks after 1.0: Orion Belt 1.1.0 on July 30 and 1.2.0 on July 31. 1.1 is about seeing what the gateway does. 1.2 is about getting it installed.

1.1.0: observability and reporting​

OpenTelemetry tracing​

The gateway and agents can emit OTLP traces to any collector (OpenTelemetry Collector, Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb). One trace covers an SSH session end to end: authorization at the gateway, the gateway → agent hop, and the agent → target hop. When a connection is slow, the trace shows which hop. It's off by default and costs nothing when disabled. Details in Tracing SSH sessions with OpenTelemetry.

Report exports​

Audit and security reports export as PDF for reviewers, CSV for spreadsheets, and a SIEM-oriented format for log pipelines, from the console or the API.

Usage analytics​

A dashboard with access volume, approval latency and the most used targets. It answers "who actually uses production access, and how long do approvals take?" without exporting the audit log first.

Notification policy​

Users choose which notifications they get; admins set an org-wide policy that bounds those choices. A user can't opt out of something the policy requires.

Go SDK​

A Go client for the public API, for scripts and integrations that would otherwise hand-roll HTTP calls. First-pass Python, JavaScript and .NET clients ship alongside it as a starting point.

1.2.0: install and day-to-day​

One-line server installer​

scripts/install-server.sh installs the server from the distribution packages, sets up a local PostgreSQL (or reuses one, or takes a DSN), asks for the public URL and WebAuthn settings, enables the systemd or OpenRC service, and writes an osh client config for the user who ran it.

The public URL is now a first-class setting (server.public_url). The Add agent flow and the setup wizard use it, so generated agent install commands point at the right address.

In-app notifications​

Access request events appear in the console's notification bell. Admins also get a notice when WebAuthn is enabled in the config but fails to start, which used to fail silently.

Fixes​

  • Agents and users with recorded sessions or grants can be hard-deleted; the schema repairs its foreign keys on migrate.
  • Deleting an agent through the API also removes its synthetic agent user, as the CLI already did.

Known limitations in 1.2.0​

From the release notes, so you can plan around them:

  • Revoking or pausing an agent can be undone when the agent reconnects.
  • POST /public/register/client still accepts is_admin for lab bootstrap; lock it down in production.
  • Recording retention targets cast files by modification time and may leave encrypted files or session rows behind.

Upgrade​

Install 1.2.0 and restart. Migrations run on start.

Release notes: v1.1.0 · v1.2.0

entry.title: How to audit SSH access on Linux — what sshd, auditd, tlog and a gateway each record
entry.summary: A practical comparison of the ways to audit SSH sessions on Linux — sshd logs, auditd, pam_tty_audit, tlog, script and an SSH gateway — with what each one captures, what it misses, and how to combine them.
entry.content:
To audit SSH access on Linux you need three things: who logged in, what they did, and proof that the record wasn't changed by the person being audited. No single host tool gives you all three. This guide compares the common options and shows where a gateway like Orion Belt fits.

The short answer​

ToolWho logged inWhat they typedWhat they sawSurvives root on the host
sshd logs (LogLevel VERBOSE)Yes, with key fingerprintNoNoNo
auditd (execve rules)Yes (auid)Commands run, not keystrokesNoOnly if shipped off-host at once
pam_tty_auditYesKeystrokesNoOnly if shipped off-host at once
tlogYesYesYesOnly if shipped off-host at once
script / shell historySelf-reportedPartlyscript onlyNo
SSH gateway recordingYesYesYesYes: recorded before the host

The last column is the one auditors care about. Anything recorded on the target can be edited by whoever has root on the target, and the people you most need to audit usually do.

sshd logs: the baseline​

Set LogLevel VERBOSE in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. sshd then logs the fingerprint of the key used for each login, not only the username, so you can tell which of a shared account's keys was used (sshd_config(5)).

It tells you nothing about what happened after login.

auditd: commands, not sessions​

The Linux audit framework can log every execve call with the login UID (auid), which survives sudo:

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k user-commands

You get a reliable list of programs run and their arguments. You do not get keystrokes inside interactive programs (vim, psql, mysql) or anything the user saw on screen. Volume is high; plan for log shipping.

pam_tty_audit: keystrokes​

pam_tty_audit records TTY input into the audit log (pam_tty_audit(8)). It catches keystrokes in interactive programs. By default it skips input typed with echo off, such as passwords; the log_passwd option records that too. Output is not recorded, so a reviewer sees what was typed but not what the system answered.

tlog: full terminal recording on the host​

tlog records terminal input and output as JSON and can replay it. It's the most complete host-side option and is packaged on RHEL and Fedora. Like everything on this list so far, it runs on the target, under the target's root.

script and shell history: not evidence​

script and ~/.bash_history are useful for the user. They are written by the user, can be turned off by the user, and prove nothing.

Recording at the gateway​

An SSH gateway sits between the user and the host and records the session stream as it passes through. The target never holds the recording, so root on the target can't alter it.

In Orion Belt the gateway records every SSH session, optionally compressed and encrypted at rest with a retention period. Admins can watch a session live and replay it in the console. Each session is tied to the user's identity at the gateway, not to the shared Unix account on the host, and to the approval that allowed it if access was requested just in time.

Targets also don't need an inbound SSH port: the agent dials out to the gateway.

A layered setup that holds up​

  1. Gateway recording for every interactive session: the tamper-resistant record of who did what.
  2. auditd on hosts, shipped off-host, for commands run by services, cron jobs and anything that didn't come through the gateway.
  3. sshd LogLevel VERBOSE, to spot direct logins that bypassed the gateway. Once the gateway is in place, there shouldn't be any.

FAQ​

Can I record SSH sessions without installing anything on the server? Yes, at a gateway. Host-side tools (tlog, pam_tty_audit) need packages and configuration on every server.

Does auditd record what a user typed in vim or psql? No. auditd records the programs started (execve). Keystrokes need pam_tty_audit or full session recording.

Where should SSH audit logs be stored? Off the host, as soon as they're written, somewhere the audited users can't write to. A gateway does this by design.

Related​

  • Why session recording is hard
  • SSH bastion vs PAM
  • Try Orion Belt in 10 minutes

entry.title: Orion Belt vs Teleport — a practical Teleport alternative for SSH PAM
entry.summary: Compare Orion Belt and Teleport for self-hosted privileged access. When a lighter SSH bastion/PAM gateway wins, when Teleport’s broader platform is worth it, plus Boundary and classic bastions.
entry.content:
Short version: Orion Belt is a self-hosted SSH access gateway with PAM workflows. Teleport is a broad zero-trust access platform. If you mainly need mediated SSH, recording, JIT, and MFA — without inbound ports on every host or a large ops surface — Orion Belt is the lighter Teleport alternative.

This comparison is for practitioners evaluating open source PAM / self-hosted privileged access options for SSH, not a dunk contest. Licensing differs; verify current Teleport terms for your use case. Orion Belt is open source under the AGPL v3.0 since 1.5.0 (details).

Who should read this​

  • Teams searching for a Teleport alternative focused on SSH
  • Homelab and SMB operators who find Teleport’s surface area large
  • Security engineers comparing bastion vs platform approaches

Side-by-side​

DimensionOrion BeltTeleportHashiCorp BoundaryTraditional bastion
Primary jobSSH PAM / bastion gatewayMulti-protocol zero-trust accessIdentity-aware session brokeringNetwork jump point
Protocols (typical)SSH / SCP (focused)SSH, K8s, DB, web, Windows, …Many via targets/workersWhatever you tunnel
How targets are reachedAgents dial out (reverse SSH)Node agents / tunnels / IoTWorkers / proxiesInbound to bastion; often inbound to hosts
Inbound on targetsNot required for agent pathDepends on modeDepends on layoutCommon
Session recordingYes (+ live watch)YesYes (with recording path)DIY
JIT / approvalsBuilt-in (+ ChatOps)Access requests / rolesVia IdP / workflowsRare
MFATOTP + WebAuthn; FIDO SSH keysStrong IdP / MFA storyVia IdPDIY
AuthorizationReBAC (+ optional OpenFGA)RBAC / roles / traitsIAM-centricOS users / keys
SSH CAOptional built-inFirst-class cert storyDifferent modelManual / none
Ops weightSmaller SSH-focused deployLarger platformMedium–largeSmall but feature-poor
HostingSelf-hostedSelf-hosted or cloudSelf-hosted or HCPSelf-hosted

Architecture contrast​

Traditional bastion​

Operator → (SSH) → Bastion → (SSH) → Target

You still manage keys, often lack recording/JIT, and frequently still expose SSH somewhere on the path.

Orion Belt​

Operator → Gateway ← (reverse SSH) ← Agent on target

The target initiates the tunnel. The gateway brokers sessions, enforces policy, and can record or live-watch. Background: Why reverse SSH agents.

Teleport-shaped platforms​

Powerful and broad: many protocols, deep identity integration, large feature surface — and correspondingly more to deploy, learn, and operate.

When to choose Orion Belt​

Choose Orion Belt if most of these are true:

  • Privileged access is mostly SSH
  • You want no inbound SSH on application hosts
  • You want recording + live watch + JIT without a PAM appliance
  • You prefer self-hosted, Linux-first, inspectable code
  • You accept a narrower scope today (OIDC, HA, other protocols on the roadmap)

Hands-on: Try in 10 minutes.

When Teleport (or similar) is a better fit​

Choose Teleport if you need:

  • First-class Kubernetes / DB / Windows / web access in one product now
  • A large ecosystem and org-wide zero-trust program already centered on that tool
  • Features Orion Belt has not shipped yet

When Boundary fits better​

Boundary shines when the center of gravity is identity + credential brokering in a HashiCorp world — not “SSH bastion with PAM workflows” as the primary UX.

Security tradeoffs (reverse agents)​

Gain: targets need outbound reachability to the gateway, not inbound SSH from attackers’ scan range.
Cost: offline agents are unreachable; the gateway is a high-value control plane — harden it, encrypt recordings, require MFA for admins.

SEO-style FAQ​

Is Orion Belt a Teleport alternative?
For SSH-centric self-hosted PAM/bastion needs, yes. For full multi-protocol zero trust, Teleport remains broader.

Is Orion Belt open source?
Yes, since 1.5.0: GNU AGPL v3.0 only, an OSI-approved license. Free to use, self-host and run commercially; if you distribute it or offer a modified version over a network, you publish your source under the same license. Releases 1.0 to 1.4 were Apache 2.0 + Commons Clause.

Can I migrate from a jump host?
Yes: enroll agents, move humans to user+host@gateway, turn on recording, then tighten inbound SSH. See bastion vs PAM.

Try before you debate​

git clone https://github.com/orion-belt-dev/orion-belt.git
cd orion-belt
./scripts/docker-quickstart.sh

entry.content:
Orion Belt v1.0 is out: a stable, self-hosted SSH access gateway with PAM workflows. Reverse agents, session recording, live watch, JIT approvals, MFA/WebAuthn, ReBAC, optional SSH CA, Linux packages, and a web console — without a SaaS dependency.

This is the release note for operators who have been waiting for a version line we are willing to call production-shaped for the SSH slice.

What “v1.0” means here​

  • SSH proxy / bastion path we will not casually break
  • Documented Docker quickstart and package installs
  • Recording + live watch on the gateway path
  • JIT + ChatOps approvals
  • MFA options for the console
  • ReBAC (optional OpenFGA)
  • Optional SSH CA
  • OpenAPI + observability docs in the main repo

Still on the roadmap (not pretend-done): OIDC, HA, additional protocols. Honesty > checkbox theater — lessons.

Positioning​

Teleport-like SSH access control — without opening inbound ports on every host or adopting a large platform.

entry.summary: We are looking for the first ~20 teams and labs running Orion Belt v1.0. Get install help, influence the roadmap, and help shape a self-hosted Teleport alternative for SSH.
entry.content:
GitHub stars are a lagging indicator. The leading indicator we care about is simple: are serious people deploying Orion Belt and telling us what breaks?

This is an open call for early operators — roughly the first twenty labs or small teams running v1.0 as a real self-hosted SSH PAM / bastion path.

Who we want​

  • Homelab / self-hosting users with more than one Linux box
  • Small company SRE/DevOps teams needing recording + JIT without SaaS
  • Security engineers evaluating a Teleport alternative for SSH-only scope
  • People willing to file reproducible bugs (Docker quickstart welcome)

Who we are not optimizing for (yet)​

  • Enterprises needing HA + OIDC + multi-protocol on day one
  • Teams whose policy rules out AGPL software (license notes; Orion Belt moved from Commons Clause to the AGPL v3.0 in 1.5.0)
  • Drive-by “please add my niche protocol” without deploying SSH first

What you get​

  • Direct help on Discord when agents will not dial out
  • Faster eyes on your issues and PRs
  • Input on roadmap sequencing (OIDC, HA, etc.)
  • Optional public credit as an early operator

What we ask​

  1. Complete Try in 10 minutes
  2. Leave it running on something you actually use (even a homelab VM)
  3. Open GitHub issues with versions, logs, and repro steps
  4. Tell us if docs lied

How to raise your hand​

  • Message in Discord
  • Open a GitHub Discussion
  • Or comment on an issue that you are running v1.0 in anger

Metrics we track privately for the first month: install attempts, active deployments, external issues — not vanity follower counts. Background: lessons building PAM.

entry.title: Lessons learned building a self-hosted SSH PAM gateway
entry.summary: Practical lessons from building Orion Belt — access control vs audit, UX for JIT, reverse tunnel tradeoffs, licensing honesty, and keeping a 10-minute install path sacred.
entry.content:
Orion Belt v1.0 is our line in the sand for a stable self-hosted SSH PAM slice. These are the lessons that shaped it — useful if you are building similar infrastructure or evaluating whether our tradeoffs match yours.

1. Access control is easy compared to audit​

ReBAC graphs are approachable. Faithful, replayable, retainable session recordings are not. Budget engineering time accordingly. Deep dive: Session recording is hard.

2. UX beats feature count for JIT​

If temporary access takes longer than sharing a key, standing keys win. ChatOps approvals and a short CLI/UI path matter more than a twelfth policy DSL. See JIT access.

3. Reverse tunnels move risk; they don’t delete it​

Agents dialing out remove inbound SSH on targets and concentrate trust on the gateway. Harden the gateway like a directory service. Explained in Why reverse SSH agents.

4. Optional complexity must stay optional​

SSH CA, OpenFGA, and WebAuthn are valuable. None of them should block the first recorded session. Optional flags exist so labs stay fast (SSH CA, MFA).

5. License clarity is a security feature​

People evaluating PAM software are professionally paranoid. Commons Clause disclosed early builds trust even when it loses some adopters. License FAQ.

Update, November 2026: in 1.5.0 we moved to the AGPL v3.0, an OSI-approved license. Why.

6. Protect the 10-minute path like an API​

Every feature PR should ask: did we break docker-quickstart → agent → Sessions? If yes, fix or document before merge. Install path design.

7. Say no to protocol sprawl in v1​

Kubernetes and database proxies are real needs. Shipping a mediocre version of each would dilute the SSH promise. Roadmap honesty > checkbox theater. Comparison mindset: vs Teleport.

8. Dual packaging is worth it​

Docker converts; packages retain. Packages and labs.

What we want next from the community​

Sharp issues from people who deployed something — not drive-by feature wishes. If that is you: early operators.
